passage: In her third week at the marketing firm, Manjula watched team meetings the way she once watched exam invigilators. Nobody had told her the rules, but she was starting to see them. The juniors waited until Rekha ma'am finished before speaking. Emails to the client always copied the account head, though no policy said so. Hrithik, a colleague two desks away, noticed her staring. “You're not doing anything wrong,” he said quietly. “Just watch who gets copied and who speaks first.” That night she typed a list into her phone: reply to seniors within two hours; don't interrupt Rekha ma'am; ask Hrithik before sending anything to the client. Her stomach still tightened every time she pressed send.

qa.q: Who waited until Rekha ma'am finished before speaking?
qa.a: The juniors waited until Rekha ma'am finished before speaking.

qa.q: Why did Manjula watch team meetings so closely?
qa.a: Manjula seems anxious about making a misstep, since nobody had told her the rules and her stomach tightened every time she pressed send.

qa.q: What could Manjula do besides watching and keeping a list?
qa.a: Manjula could ask one trusted colleague, like Hrithik, to explain the habits she is unsure about and check her guesses against what he says.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have felt when he saw Manjula staring at the meeting?
qa.a: Hrithik probably recognised what a newcomer's worry looks like and wanted to reassure her, which fits his quiet, “You're not doing anything wrong.”

grounding: A new graduate learns the unwritten rules of the office by watching closely, and feels anxious about missteps.

passage:
“Pradeep, who am I supposed to copy on the vendor mail?” Urmila whispered at the coffee machine. “Nobody told me.”
Pradeep glanced at the corridor. “Nobody tells anyone. Copy the team lead on anything that goes outside. It's not written anywhere.”
“And in the Monday meeting? Sunita spoke over me last week.”
“Sunita speaks over everyone. Wait until the lead finishes, then say it plainly. If it matters, send it in writing after.”
Sunita walked in and both went quiet. She smiled, took her tea and asked, “New-joiner questions?” Urmila's ears went hot. “Something like that.”
“Ask me anytime,” Sunita said, and left.
Urmila let out a breath. “See?” Pradeep said. “Half the rules are people being nervous.”

qa.q: Whom did Pradeep say to copy on anything that goes outside?
qa.a: Pradeep said to copy the team lead on anything that goes outside.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's ears go hot when Sunita walked in?
qa.a: Urmila seems embarrassed at being overheard asking about Sunita's habit of speaking over others, and worried about a misstep.

qa.q: What could Urmila try in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Urmila could wait until the lead finishes, say her point plainly, and send it in writing afterwards if it matters.

qa.q: How might Sunita have felt when she asked, “New-joiner questions?”
qa.a: Sunita seems friendly and at ease, offering help, and may not know how her interrupting comes across.

grounding: A new graduate discovers that the real rules of the office are unwritten, asks quietly and feels anxious about missteps.

passage: Mahima, you asked how the new job's going. Honestly? Jeevan here is learning a secret language. Nobody told me you always copy Venkat sir on client emails, even though he never replies. I found out when my manager forwarded one of mine back with just 'Loop V.' And in meetings, juniors don't talk until the director has spoken, even if you know the answer. I spoke first in week one. Nobody said anything, but the room went cold, and my senior, Farah, gave me this tiny head shake. Now I sit there watching everyone like a hawk: who nods, who laughs, who leaves first. I'm tired by six just from the watching. Is that normal, or am I overthinking?

qa.q: What did Jeevan's manager write when forwarding the email back?
qa.a: Just 'Loop V.'

qa.q: How is Jeevan feeling about the office's hidden rules?
qa.a: Jeevan feels anxious and watchful, afraid of more missteps, and is worn out by six from all the watching.

qa.q: What would you advise Jeevan to do?
qa.a: Ask Farah or another friendly senior for a short chat about how meetings and emails usually work, instead of guessing alone.

qa.q: What might Farah have meant by the tiny head shake?
qa.a: Farah may have been warning Jeevan kindly about an unwritten rule, rather than scolding.

grounding: A new graduate discovers the office's unwritten rules about emails and speaking order and watches anxiously for missteps.

passage: Day one: Nilesh left the office at 6:00 sharp, as his offer letter said. The next morning Reena, a senior on his team, said lightly, 'Leaving early yesterday?' He went red and didn't know what to say. Day four: he stayed until 7:30, watching when others packed up. The rule seemed to be: never leave before the team lead. He also noticed that people used the manager's first name in chat, never in meetings. He wrote all this in a notebook, feeling like a spy and a fool. Week three, Friday: Reena saw his list and laughed. 'Half of these are real. The leaving one, no. Our lead stays late because she has calls with another time zone. Leave at six if your work's done.' Nilesh crossed it out, embarrassed and very relieved.

qa.q: What time did Nilesh leave on day one?
qa.a: At 6:00 sharp.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel while writing the rules in a notebook?
qa.a: He felt anxious and foolish, like a spy and a fool, trying hard not to misstep.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh most, and what could he try sooner next time?
qa.a: Reena's honest check of his list; next time he could ask a friendly senior early instead of guessing for weeks.

qa.q: Why might Reena have laughed at the list?
qa.a: Reena probably found it both funny and a little sweet, seeing how hard he was trying, and wanted to set him straight kindly.

grounding: Over three weeks a new graduate anxiously decodes unwritten office rules, some real and some imagined.

passage: Jahnavi, first-job nerves? Let your Minakshi atya tell you about the insurance office in Nagpur, back in 1996. On my first day I sat in the empty chair by the window. Nobody said a word, but by lunch the whole section was whispering. That was the head clerk's chair, and nobody sat there, even when he was on leave. I also didn't know that files went to the officer only after the head clerk initialled them. I sent one straight up, and it came back with a note in red. I cried in the ladies' washroom. Then old Sulochana-bai took me for tea and explained the whole unwritten map: whose chair, which file, when to speak. After that I watched carefully, and asked her before guessing. Find your Sulochana-bai, beta.

qa.q: Whose chair did young Minakshi sit in on the first day?
qa.a: The head clerk's chair, by the window.

qa.q: How did young Minakshi feel after the file came back with a red note?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious about the misstep, and cried in the washroom.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Minakshi?
qa.a: Sulochana-bai taking her for tea and explaining the unwritten rules, after which she asked before guessing.

qa.q: How might Sulochana-bai have seen the new clerk?
qa.a: Sulochana-bai likely saw a nervous newcomer making common mistakes and chose to guide her kindly.

grounding: An aunt recalls her first office job, where unwritten rules caused anxious missteps until an older colleague explained them.

passage: Kamal's first real deadline arrived on his ninth day at the logistics firm: the vendor summary, due at five. At 4:40 he hit send, addressed to his manager, Ms Rao, alone. Within a minute Vishal, two desks over, leaned across. "You didn't copy Farooq sir?" "Is that a rule?" "Not written anywhere. But he handles the vendors, so he expects it." Kamal's neck went hot. He resent the mail with an apologetic line and then sat very still, replaying every email he had sent that week. In the 5:30 meeting he noticed that nobody spoke before Ms Rao did, and that Vishal waited for Farooq sir to finish before disagreeing. Kamal opened his notebook to a fresh page and wrote a title at the top: "Things no one says."

qa.q: When was the vendor summary due?
qa.a: It was due at five.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling after Vishal pointed out the missing name?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious; his neck went hot and he replayed every email of the week, afraid of other missteps.

qa.q: What small step helped Kamal start learning the office's hidden rules?
qa.a: Watching the meeting closely and noting patterns on a "Things no one says" page, while asking a friendly colleague like Vishal when unsure.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Kamal's mistake?
qa.a: Vishal probably sees it as an ordinary new-joiner slip and wants to save Kamal trouble, not embarrass him.

grounding: Shows a new graduate discovering under deadline pressure that the office's real rules are unwritten, and watching anxiously to learn them.
